title: Circular motion, rotation and gravitation
blurb: Explain centripetal acceleration and force, calculate torque, period and frequency, and apply the inverse-square law of gravitation.
question: A car rounds an icy curve at a steady speed and slides off it. Which way was it accelerating before it slid, which way did it slide, and how would the pull of gravity on a satellite change if its distance from Earth's center doubled?

teach.body: Formally, uniform circular motion is motion in a circle at constant speed. The speed is steady, but the velocity's direction changes every instant, so the object accelerates toward the center: centripetal (center-seeking) acceleration, a_c = v²/r. In plain English: to go around a bend, something must keep pulling you inward. That inward net force is the centripetal force, F_c = mv²/r. It is not a new kind of force; a real force supplies it.

head: Situation
Real force pulling inward
rows: Rider at the top of a loop
Normal force from the seat (plus gravity)

teach.body: a_c = v²/r and F_c = mv²/r (the stem gives these). Speed is squared: double v and the force needed quadruples. A larger radius at the same speed needs less force. Period T is the time for one revolution; frequency f = 1/T, in hertz (revolutions per second). Example: a 1,000 kg car on a 50 m curve at 20 m/s has a_c = 400 ÷ 50 = 8.0 m/s² and needs F_c = 8,000 N of friction.

rows.label: A real force?
values: No: the felt effect of inertia

teach.caption: Release a whirled ball and it flies off in a straight line tangent to the circle, the direction it was moving at that instant.

teach.body: Torque is the turning effect of a force: τ = rF, with the force perpendicular to the lever arm r, in N·m. The same force farther from the pivot gives more torque, which is why wrenches are long and doorknobs sit far from the hinges. Rotational inertia is resistance to a change in spin; it grows when mass sits farther from the axis. A spinning skater who pulls her arms in spins faster because her angular momentum is conserved.

teach.h: A 20 N push at different distances from the pivot
teach.caption: τ = rF: five times the distance, five times the torque.

teach.body: Every mass attracts every other mass: F = Gm₁m₂/r², where r is the distance between centers and G is given (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²). Force is proportional to each mass and inversely proportional to the SQUARE of the distance. Astronauts in orbit feel weightless not because gravity is absent but because they and their station are in continuous free fall around Earth.

head: Change
New force
teach.caption: Square the distance factor, never the mass factor. Two masses attracting with 36 N: triple the distance and the force is 36 ÷ 9 = 4.0 N.

teach.h: Scenario: Grace on the icy curve
teach.body: Grace, a nursing applicant, drives a 1,200 kg car around a curve of radius 40 m at 20 m/s. The car needs a_c = 400 ÷ 40 = 10 m/s² toward the center, so friction must supply 1,200 × 10 = 12,000 N. On ice the tires cannot grip that hard. With too little inward force the car stops turning and slides off in a straight line along the tangent, not straight outward.

teach.text: Constant speed in a circle is still acceleration, and it points inward. Centrifugal force is not the real force; a released object goes along the tangent. Gravity is inverse-SQUARE: double the distance gives one fourth of the force, not half. Orbiting astronauts still feel gravity. Torque depends on where the force is applied.

items: Uniform circular motion: constant speed, acceleration toward the center (a_c = v²/r).
Centripetal force F_c = mv²/r comes from a real force: tension, friction, gravity or a normal force.
f = 1/T; double the speed and the centripetal force quadruples.
Torque τ = rF: a longer lever arm gives more turning effect.
Gravity F = Gm₁m₂/r²: double r gives F ÷ 4; orbiting means continuous free fall.

summary: You can now explain why an object moving in a circle at constant speed accelerates toward the center, name the real force that supplies the centripetal force and predict the tangent path when it stops. You can also calculate torque, period and frequency and scale gravitational force with the inverse-square law.

A.q: What supplies the centripetal force that keeps a satellite in orbit around Earth?
A.why: Gravity pulls the satellite toward Earth's center, supplying the inward (centripetal) force for its curved path.

whyNot.0: Centrifugal force is not a real force; the real inward force is gravity.
whyNot.1: There is almost no air at orbital height, and friction would act along the path, not inward.
whyNot.3: Inertia keeps the satellite moving straight; gravity is what bends its path into a circle.

A.q: A wheel turns 4 times per second. What is its period?
A.why: Frequency f = 4 Hz, so the period T = 1/f = 1/4 = 0.25 s.

whyNot.1: 4.0 is the frequency in hertz, not the period in seconds.
whyNot.3: Slips a decimal place the other way in 1 ÷ 4.

A.q: If the distance between the centers of two masses is doubled, the gravitational force between them becomes:
A.why: Gravity is inverse-square: F is proportional to 1/r², so doubling r divides F by 2² = 4.

whyNot.3: Four is the right factor, but the force decreases with distance.

B.q: A 0.50 kg ball on a string moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.80 m at 4.0 m/s. What tension supplies the centripetal force? (F_c = mv²/r)

whyNot.1: Multiplies by r instead of dividing (0.50 × 16 × 0.80).

B.q: A mechanic cannot loosen a stuck bolt with a short wrench. Which change gives more torque for the same push?
options: A wrench twice as long, pushed at its end
Pushing nearer the bolt end of the handle
Pushing along the handle toward the bolt
A heavier wrench of the same length
B.why: τ = rF with the force perpendicular to the arm. Doubling the lever arm doubles the torque for the same force.

whyNot.1: A shorter lever arm gives less torque.
whyNot.2: A push along the handle has no perpendicular part, so it produces almost no torque.
whyNot.3: The wrench's mass does not change the torque from the push; the lever arm does.

B.q: A satellite's distance from Earth's center is halved. How does Earth's gravitational pull on it change?
options: It becomes one fourth as large
B.why: F is proportional to 1/r². Halving r multiplies the force by 2² = 4.

whyNot.0: Treats gravity as 1/r; the square makes the factor 4.
whyNot.3: One fourth is the result for doubling the distance, not halving it.

C.q: A car rounds a curve at 10 m/s with a centripetal acceleration of 2.0 m/s². What is the radius of the curve? (a_c = v²/r)

whyNot.1: Multiplies v² by a_c instead of dividing.
whyNot.2: Divides by 2a_c (100 ÷ 4.0), as if the formula carried a 2.

C.q: Two asteroids attract each other with a force of 90 N. If both masses are tripled and the distance between their centers is also tripled, what is the new force?
C.why: Masses: × 3 × 3 = × 9. Distance tripled: ÷ 3² = ÷ 9. Net change × 9 ÷ 9 = × 1, so the force stays 90 N.

whyNot.0: Counts only one tripled mass and leaves out the distance change.
whyNot.2: Counts both mass changes but leaves out the distance change.
whyNot.3: Applies the distance change but leaves out both mass changes.

C.q: A ball is whirled in a horizontal circle. The string breaks when the ball is at the north point of the circle, moving east. Which way does the ball move just after?
C.why: With no inward force, the ball keeps the velocity it had at that instant: east, along the tangent to the circle.

whyNot.0: There is no outward force; the 'centrifugal' feeling is inertia.
whyNot.1: The inward pull ended when the string broke.
whyNot.3: Nothing pushes the ball outward, so it does not drift north.

reteach.title: Mud flying off a bike tire
reteach.question: Ride a bike through a puddle and mud sprays off the tire. Why does it fly off forward and up in straight lines, not outward like spokes?

blocks.body: While mud sticks to the tire, the sticking force pulls it inward and it rides around in a circle. The moment the mud breaks free, nothing pulls it inward any more, so it carries on in a straight line in the direction it was already moving: along the tangent. Faster wheels need a stronger inward pull (it goes with v²), which is why mud flies off more at speed.

blocks.h: Before and after the mud breaks free

blocks.text: Nothing throws the mud outward. Inertia keeps it going straight once the inward force is gone.

explain.body: In uniform circular motion the acceleration (and net force) points to the center of the circle.

test.q: A runner on a curved section of track keeps a constant speed. Which way does her acceleration point?
options: Away from the center of the curve
Toward the center of the curve
It is zero at constant speed
test.why: Her direction keeps changing, so she accelerates toward the center of the curve.

whyNot.0: The net force and acceleration point inward, not outward.
whyNot.2: A forward acceleration would increase her speed, which is constant.
whyNot.3: Changing direction is an acceleration even at constant speed.

explain.body: a_c = v²/r. Halve the speed and the centripetal acceleration falls to one fourth; double it and it rises fourfold.

test.q: A bus's speed on a curve drops from 20 m/s to 10 m/s. How does its centripetal acceleration change?
options: It becomes one half as large
It becomes one fourth as large
test.why: a_c is proportional to v². Halving v multiplies a_c by (½)² = ¼.

whyNot.0: Treats a_c as proportional to v; it goes with v².
whyNot.1: Slowing down reduces the centripetal acceleration.
whyNot.2: a_c depends on speed, so it changes.

explain.body: τ = rF, force perpendicular to the lever arm, in N·m. Multiply, never divide.

test.q: A 60 N force is applied perpendicular to a wrench, 0.25 m from the bolt. What torque does it produce?

whyNot.1: Divides the force by the distance (60 ÷ 0.25).
whyNot.2: Gives the force alone; torque also depends on the lever arm.
whyNot.3: Halves the product; torque has no ½ factor.

explain.body: Multiply the distance by k and the gravitational force is divided by k².

test.q: Two masses attract each other with a force of 50 N. If the distance between their centers is multiplied by 5, what is the new force?

whyNot.2: Multiplies by 5; a greater distance weakens gravity.
whyNot.3: Divides by 5³ = 125; the distance is squared, not cubed.
